overview.title: Plotting the training curves: clear overfitting
overview.section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset
overview.main_topic: Plotting training and validation accuracy and loss from the History object (listing 8.16) and interpreting figure 8.9 as a textbook case of overfitting
overview.central_idea: Training accuracy climbs to nearly 100% and training loss falls toward zero, while validation accuracy peaks around 80% and validation loss stops improving early — the signature of overfitting on 2,000 images; the model will therefore be evaluated from the checkpoint saved before overfitting began.
overview.importance: Reading train/validation curves is the main diagnostic for generalization. This page establishes the baseline problem — overfitting — that data augmentation (section 8.2.5) and pretrained models (section 8.3) will address.
learning_objectives: Extract per-epoch metrics from history.history and plot them with matplotlib
Recognize the visual signature of overfitting in accuracy and loss curves
Relate the validation-loss minimum to the epoch saved by ModelCheckpoint
Explain why the test evaluation uses the reloaded checkpoint

summary:
**Listing 8.16** pulls four lists from the `History` object returned by `fit()` — `accuracy`, `val_accuracy`, `loss`, `val_loss` — builds `epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)`, and draws two matplotlib figures: training accuracy (red dashed, `"r--"`) vs validation accuracy (blue solid, `"b"`), then, after `plt.figure()` opens a new figure, training vs validation loss in the same styles.

**Figure 8.9** shows the result over 50 epochs. Reading the plots (approximately): training accuracy rises from about 0.52 to essentially 1.0 by around epoch 35–40; validation accuracy rises with it at first, then levels off around 0.80–0.83. Training loss falls from ~0.69 (the loss of a 50/50 guess, ln 2) to nearly 0; validation loss falls to about 0.5 and then climbs and becomes erratic, with a spike of ~1.28 near epoch 37 and ~0.95 at epoch 50.

The authors' reading: these plots are **characteristic of overfitting**. Training accuracy increases linearly until it reaches nearly 100%, whereas validation accuracy peaks around 80%. The validation loss reaches its minimum after only 10 epochs and then stalls, whereas the training loss keeps decreasing linearly. (In the printed figure the validation-loss minimum looks closer to epoch 20 — see the review flag — but the conclusion is the same: the model memorizes the 2,000 training images while generalization stops improving.)

Finally, the authors announce the test evaluation: they will **reload the model from its saved file** — the `ModelCheckpoint` file from p.274, which holds the lowest-validation-loss epoch — so that it is evaluated as it was before it started overfitting. The test accuracy (78.6%) follows on p.276.

paragraphs.excerpt: These plots are characteristic of overfitting. The training accuracy increases linearly over time
paragraphs.what_it_says: The curves show overfitting: training accuracy rises linearly to nearly 100% while validation accuracy peaks around 80%; validation loss reaches its minimum after about 10 epochs and stalls while training loss keeps decreasing linearly.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The growing gap between training and validation metrics means the network is fitting idiosyncrasies of the 2,000 training images that do not transfer to new images. Once validation loss stops falling, further training only improves memorization. A rising validation loss while validation accuracy stays flat also means the model becomes over-confident on the validation examples it gets wrong.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the diagnosis that motivates data augmentation (p.276) and the use of pretrained models (section 8.3). It also justifies the checkpoint strategy of p.274.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Loss at epoch 1 ≈ 0.69 ≈ ln 2, the binary crossentropy of predicting 0.5 for every image — the expected starting point for a balanced binary problem.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: Training performance keeps improving while validation performance stalls or worsens.
concepts.intuition: The model memorizes the training images instead of learning what makes a cat a cat.
concepts.technical: Diagnosed by the divergence of training and validation loss curves; here validation accuracy plateaus near 80% while training accuracy reaches ~100%.
concepts.significance: With only 2,000 training images it is the number-one concern (p.276).
concepts.misconception: Overfitting does not mean validation accuracy must fall; it can plateau while validation loss rises.

concepts.name: Training and validation curves
concepts.definition: Per-epoch plots of loss and metrics on training and validation data.
concepts.intuition: A health chart of the training run.
concepts.significance: The standard way to pick the best epoch and detect over-/underfitting.
concepts.misconception: A low training loss alone says nothing about generalization.

concepts.name: Reloading the best checkpoint
concepts.definition: Restoring the model saved at the lowest validation loss for evaluation.
concepts.intuition: Rewinding to the best save point.
concepts.significance: Evaluates the model 'as it was before it started overfitting'.
concepts.misconception: The last-epoch model is not the one you should evaluate here.

code.title: Displaying curves of loss and accuracy during training
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
accuracy = history.history["accuracy"]
val_accuracy = history.history["val_accuracy"]
loss = history.history["loss"]
val_loss = history.history["val_loss"]
epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)
plt.plot(epochs, accuracy, "r--", label="Training accuracy")
plt.plot(epochs, val_accuracy, "b", label="Validation accuracy")
plt.title("Training and validation accuracy")
plt.legend()
plt.figure()
plt.plot(epochs, loss, "r--", label="Training loss")
plt.plot(epochs, val_loss, "b", label="Validation loss")
plt.title("Training and validation loss")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Plots the per-epoch training and validation accuracy in one figure and the losses in a second figure (figure 8.9).

line_explanations.explanation: history.history is a dict of lists, one value per epoch, keyed by metric name; 'val_' prefixes come from validation_data.
Accuracy figure: red dashed line for training, solid blue for validation, title and legend.

Loss figure with the same styling; show() displays both.

deeper.title: Reading figure 8.9 epoch by epoch
deeper.body:
Approximate values read from the printed figure (not stated in the text):

| phase | epochs | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| learning | 1–~10 | train and val accuracy rise together from ~0.55 to ~0.70; both losses drop from 0.69 to ~0.6 |
| diverging | ~10–~22 | train accuracy keeps climbing (~0.9); val accuracy creeps to ~0.8; val loss bottoms out around 0.5 |
| memorizing | ~22–50 | train accuracy → 1.0, train loss → 0; val accuracy flat at ~0.82; val loss climbs and spikes (~1.28 at ~37) |

The saved checkpoint corresponds to the val-loss minimum.

deeper.title: Why validation loss can rise while validation accuracy stays flat
deeper.body: Beyond the book: accuracy only checks whether p is on the right side of 0.5; loss also measures confidence. As the network memorizes the training set it pushes its outputs toward 0 and 1. On validation images it still gets ~80% right, but for the ~20% it gets wrong it is now very confident, and binary crossentropy punishes a confident mistake heavily (e.g. −ln(0.01) ≈ 4.6). So the average validation loss grows even though the count of correct answers barely changes.

deeper.title: An exam analogy
deeper.body: A student who rereads the same 2,000 practice questions until they can recite every answer (training accuracy 100%) does not get better at new questions after a point (validation ~80%) and may become overconfident on the questions they misunderstand (rising validation loss). The best moment to take the real exam was earlier — which is what the checkpoint captures.

visualizations.title: Overfitting in training curves
visualizations.why: Figure 8.9 shows training and validation curves diverging; the text places the validation-loss minimum after about 10 of 50 epochs. Move the best-epoch marker to see what ModelCheckpoint would keep.

misconceptions.claim: Since training accuracy reaches nearly 100%, the model is excellent.
misconceptions.correction: Validation accuracy peaks around 80%; the near-perfect training score reflects memorization.

misconceptions.claim: Overfitting always shows up as falling validation accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: Here validation accuracy plateaus while validation loss stalls and then rises; loss is the more sensitive indicator.

misconceptions.claim: The test accuracy should be measured with the final model after 50 epochs.
misconceptions.correction: The authors reload the saved checkpoint to evaluate the model as it was before overfitting.

takeaways: history.history holds per-epoch accuracy, val_accuracy, loss and val_loss for plotting.
Figure 8.9: training accuracy → ~100% and training loss → ~0, but validation accuracy peaks around 80%.
The validation loss stops improving early (the text says after ~10 epochs) while training loss keeps falling — classic overfitting.
Both losses start near ln 2 ≈ 0.69, the loss of a 50/50 guess.
The test evaluation uses the reloaded checkpoint, i.e. the model before it overfit.

questions.question: Which pattern in figure 8.9 indicates overfitting?
options: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss stops improving
Both losses decrease together until epoch 50
Validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy throughout
questions.answer: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss stops improving
questions.explanation: That divergence is what the authors describe. Both losses do not keep decreasing together; validation accuracy is below training accuracy after the first epochs; training accuracy reaches nearly 100%.

questions.question: Around what value does the validation accuracy peak, according to the text?
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph below figure 8.9.

questions.question: Why do both loss curves start near 0.69?
questions.answer: An untrained model outputs about 0.5 for every image, and binary crossentropy at p = 0.5 is −ln 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
questions.explanation: The classes are balanced, so chance-level predictions give ln 2.

questions.question: Why do the authors reload the model from its saved file before measuring test accuracy?
questions.answer: The saved file holds the epoch with the lowest validation loss, i.e. the model before it started overfitting; the in-memory model is the overfit epoch-50 version.
questions.explanation: Follows from ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss") on p.274.

questions.question: In listing 8.16, what does plt.figure() do?
options: Starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately
Saves the accuracy plot to a file
questions.answer: Starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately
questions.explanation: It opens a fresh figure; saving would be plt.savefig, history is untouched, and plt.show() displays the plots.

questions.question: How can validation loss rise while validation accuracy stays around 80%?
questions.answer: The model becomes increasingly confident; its wrong predictions become very confident, and crossentropy penalizes them heavily, so average loss rises even if the number of correct predictions barely changes.
questions.explanation: An explanation beyond the page, consistent with figure 8.9.

questions.question: Looking at figure 8.9 yourself, at which epoch would you say the validation loss is lowest, and does it match the text's 'after only 10 epochs'?
questions.answer: In the printed figure the minimum looks closer to epochs 18–22 (~0.5); the text says 10. Either way, validation loss stops improving long before epoch 50.
questions.explanation: Practice reading curves critically; runs differ due to randomness.
